frame: Wren's diary, written the morning after a bat count.
text: Last night I went to count the bats in the old mine. Everything about it was eerie. The wind made a low moaning sound through the tunnels. Water dripped somewhere in the dark, but I couldn't see where. My torch flickered. The hairs on my arms stood up, and I kept feeling that someone was standing right behind me. When I turned around, nobody was there. I counted the bats as fast as I could. Then I ran all the way back to the boat without looking behind me. This morning Gus asked if I wanted to go back tonight for a second count. I said no thanks.

text: Before: The wall behind the island shop used to be the dullest thing I had ever seen. It was the grey of old porridge, and the paint was peeling off in sad little curls. Nobody ever stopped to look at it. After: Last week the shop owner let me paint a mural. I used hot pink for the coral, electric blue for the waves and a yellow so bright it almost hummed. I added orange fish with lime-green stripes. Now the wall is so vibrant that people walking past stop in their tracks. A kid on a scooter crashed into a bin because he was staring at it. (He was fine.) The shop owner says her sales have doubled. The Tintacle sat in front of it for an hour, flashing every colour it could, trying to keep up. frame: Wren's rescue log. The Tintacle is still flashing duck-yellow.
text: Rescue Log, Thursday. At 4 pm we got a call about a mother duck in the island car park. Her six ducklings had tumbled through a drain grate, and she couldn't reach them. When we arrived, she was frantic. She was racing back and forth across the grate, quacking at the top of her voice and flapping so hard that feathers flew everywhere. She didn't even notice the cars beeping at her. Her ducklings were peeping from the dark water below, and that only made her worse. Gus lifted the grate with a crowbar, and I lay on my stomach and scooped the ducklings out one by one with a fishing net. They were wet and cheeping, but nobody was hurt. The moment the last one was out, the mother duck went completely quiet. She tucked them under her wings and sat down as if nothing had happened. Mo says she looked a bit smug.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option

frame: A crackly message reaches the boat from a very lonely rover.
text: Day 400 on Planet Kreeb. This is Rover Pip, reporting to Earth. In every direction there is nothing but red dust and grey rock. There are no trees, no rivers and no animals. I have not seen a single living thing since I landed. My cameras still work perfectly, but there is nothing to film. I have counted every rock within a kilometre. There are 9,412, and none of them can talk. The wind blows all day, but there is nobody to hear it except me. At night the only light comes from two tiny moons, and it drops to ninety degrees below zero. This is the most desolate place I have ever explored. Yesterday I found a rock shaped like a sandwich and got very excited. It was just a rock. Sometimes I play my landing song just to hear a sound that isn't wind. Please send a friend. Even a small one. Even a toaster.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option

frame: Mo wrote about the island busking contest for the crew newsletter.
text: The Hollowgum Busking Contest had been noisy all day. Kids shouted, a dog barked at a drummer, and somebody's ukulele was badly out of tune. A juggler dropped three of his fish, and a seagull stole one. Then an old woman sat down on an upturned bucket and began to play a silver flute. Her music was soft and slow, like water running over stones. Within seconds, the whole crowd was mesmerised. Nobody talked. Nobody checked their phone. A boy holding an ice cream didn't notice it melting down his arm. Even the barking dog lay down and stared at her with its head on one side. When the last note faded, there was a long silence before anyone remembered to clap. She won first prize, a bucket of prawns, and played one more tune for free. This time the dog howled along. The juggler has asked her for flute lessons.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: so fascinated they couldn't look away

frame: Zed's diary, written by torchlight in the back of the boat.
text: Night three on Hollowgum Island. We had planned to camp at the old quarry, but from the moment we arrived, everything felt ominous. A thick fog rolled in off the water and swallowed the path behind us. The birds, which had been squawking all afternoon, suddenly went completely silent, as if someone had switched them off. Even the frogs had stopped croaking. My torch started to flicker. Far below in the quarry, something was clanking slowly, like a chain being dragged over rock. Gus said it was probably old machinery moving in the wind, but there wasn't any wind. Then the Tintacle, which never stops flashing colours, turned a flat, dull black and squeezed itself into the bottom of my backpack. Wren whispered that animals often know when something bad is about to happen. That was when we found the sign. Someone had scratched out the words 'Quarry Closed' and written underneath, in fresh red paint, 'Turn back while you can.' We didn't argue. We packed up the tents in about four minutes, which Tully says is a crew record, and we didn't stop running until we could see the lights of the boat. None of us said a word on the way back. Mo claims he wasn't scared, but he slept with the torch on.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: threatening, as if something bad is coming

frame: Tully's report on the under-12 soccer final. She's still shouting about it.
text: It all came down to the final penalty. If Harbour Heights scored, they would win the cup, but if our goalkeeper, Sami, saved it, the match would go to sudden death. Every single person in the stands was on their feet, chewing their nails or hiding their eyes behind their hands. Sami, on the other hand, looked completely nonchalant. While the striker placed the ball on the spot, Sami leaned against the goalpost, yawned and retied a bootlace as if he were waiting for a bus. He even waved to his nan in the crowd. His nan, who was the only calm person in the stands apart from Sami, waved back. Our coach was turning purple on the sideline, shouting at him to concentrate. The striker took a long run-up and blasted the ball towards the top corner. Sami simply stepped to his left and caught it against his chest. The crowd went wild, and the Harbour Heights striker sank to the grass with her hands over her face. Sami just shrugged, rolled the ball to the referee and wandered back to his line. Afterwards, a reporter asked him how he had stayed so relaxed. Sami said, 'It's only a game. Is there any orange cake left?'
answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: calm and not bothered at all

frame: Gus's lab notebook. The cover says 'Warning: contains maggots'.
text: Experiment 82: Can black soldier fly larvae eat a whole watermelon in a day? Black soldier fly larvae are fat, pale grubs that farmers sometimes use to get rid of food scraps, because they will eat almost anything. At 9 am, I placed half a watermelon in a tub containing roughly two thousand larvae. Within ten minutes, the surface of the fruit was crawling and wriggling, and I could hear a faint crunching sound, like someone eating cereal in the next room. By lunchtime, the red flesh had become a soggy pink crater. By 5 pm, nothing was left but a thin, chewed rind, and the larvae were still searching for more. When I lowered a banana skin into the tub, it vanished under a heaving pile of grubs in under a minute. These are the most voracious eaters I have ever studied. Mo asked whether they could clean up the galley after one of his cooking disasters. I said yes, as long as he didn't mind them eating the tablecloth too. Wren made me promise to keep the lid on the tub at night, just in case. Conclusion: yes, they can finish a watermelon in a day, with room to spare. Next experiment: a whole pumpkin.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option

frame: Maxx Vantablack is live-streaming again. The crew is watching on Zed's tablet.
text: 'Hey, Vantafam! Maxx here, coming to you live from Hollowgum Island, where I have just personally rescued forty-seven rare Creatures with my bare hands!' Maxx held up an empty cage and grinned at the camera. 'They were so grateful that they all flew off to freedom, which is why you can't see any of them right now. Smash that like button!' Behind him, something in the bushes squeaked, and a small furry paw poked out of a sack before Maxx quickly nudged the sack out of shot with his foot. On the boat, the crew were dubious. Gus raised one eyebrow so high it nearly left his face. Tully pointed out that catching forty-seven Creatures would take about a week, and Maxx had only arrived on the island that morning. Wren noticed that the cage still had a price sticker on it. Indi paused the stream and zoomed in on Maxx's boots, which were spotless, even though he claimed to have spent hours wading through mud. Mo pointed out that Maxx's hands, which had supposedly caught forty-seven Creatures, didn't have a single scratch. 'So,' said Mo slowly, 'we don't believe him, right?' Nobody even bothered to answer. Zed was already scrolling through the comments, looking for anyone else who had spotted the sticker.
answerWith: the text of the one correct option

frame: The island newspaper reviewed the school concert. The Tintacle went striped with shock.
prompt: Tap the words that explain what cacophony means.
answerWith: the bracketed part that answers the prompt
passage: Review: The Hollowgum Primary Band Concert. I have been to many school concerts, but nothing could have prepared me for Thursday night in [the school hall]. The Year 5 band had only been practising for two weeks, and it showed. When the conductor raised her stick, forty children started playing at once, and the result was a cacophony. Trumpets honked, drums thumped out of time and a recorder squealed like a stepped-on cat. It was [a horrible jumble of clashing sounds], and several parents in the front row quietly put their fingers in their ears. A toddler burst into tears. The school principal, who was sitting right next to me, looked as if she were trying very hard to smile. Then, halfway through the second song, something unexpected happened. Ella, the smallest player, who had only been given [the triangle], began to tap a slow, steady beat. One by one, the other players started to follow her. By the final song, the band sounded almost like music. The audience clapped for [five whole minutes], and Ella got the loudest cheer of the whole night. I would happily go again next year, although I might bring some earplugs, just in case.
